sections.heading: Start From The Ordinary Choice
sections.body: A preference is the course's way of saying that a person can put possible outcomes in an order. The idea starts before strategy, before markets, and before any game table. If a student chooses coffee over tea, or a buyer chooses one apartment over another, the model needs a clear way to record that ordering. The course is not trying to read the person's feelings. It is asking what the person's choices treat as better or worse.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Without preferences, a payoff number has no honest source. A model could still place numbers in a table, but the numbers would float without a reason. Preferences give the model a discipline: first say what outcomes the person ranks above other outcomes, then use utility or payoffs as a compact way to carry that ranking into later problems. This matters because every later result depends on what each player is counted as trying to protect, gain, avoid, or trade away.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to treat preferences as deep psychology or as a claim that people always know exactly what they want. In this course, preferences are a modeling object. They say how the model will compare outcomes inside a chosen problem. That is narrower and more useful. It lets the reader ask whether the rankings are complete enough, whether they create cycles, and whether later payoff numbers really match the story being told.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond The First Lecture
sections.body: Preferences matter in bargaining because the surplus depends on what each side values. They matter in auctions because a bid makes sense only after the bidder has a value for winning. They matter in welfare comparisons because a policy cannot be judged without saying what counts as better for someone. In topology and fixed-point arguments, preferences often enter indirectly through continuous payoff or choice maps; the existence result only means something after the model has said what better means.

applications.body: A policy model must say whose outcomes are being ranked and what tradeoffs count. Otherwise the policy conclusion can hide a value judgment inside a number.
A fixed-point proof may show that a stable choice exists, but preferences and payoffs decide what the map is. Bad rankings make the beautiful proof answer the wrong question.

title: Nash Equilibrium As A No-One-Wants-To-Move Test

sections.heading: Start From A Settled Situation
sections.body: Nash equilibrium begins with a proposed situation, not with a promise that the situation is good. Imagine two firms choosing prices, two drivers choosing routes, or two roommates choosing chores. The question is simple: if everyone else keeps doing what the proposal says, does any one person want to change alone? If the answer is no for every player, the situation passes the Nash test. If even one player wants to move, the proposed story is not stable in this sense.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Strategic stories are easy to tell and hard to trust. Someone can say prices will stay high, both sides will cooperate, or each player will choose a certain action. Nash equilibrium forces that story through a personal incentive check. Each player gets to ask whether a different available action gives a better payoff, holding the others fixed. The concept exists because prediction in a game needs more than a nice story; it needs to survive the pressure of individual deviation.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to hear equilibrium and think fair, peaceful, efficient, or morally right. Nash equilibrium does not say any of that. A traffic jam can be stable because no one driver can improve by switching routes. A bad market outcome can be stable because each firm is already doing its best against the others. The test is narrow: given what everyone else is doing, does one player want to change alone?

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond The Course
sections.body: The idea matters because many systems settle into patterns that are hard to change one person at a time. In politics, a voting rule can hold a poor outcome because each voter faces the same incentives. In networks, people may stay on a platform because others are there. In topology, Nash existence proofs often use fixed-point reasoning: a best-response map points from expected behavior to chosen behavior, and a fixed point is a place where the map sends the behavior back to itself.

applications.body: A platform can be hard to dislodge because each user chooses based on where the other users already are. Stability can come from dependence, not quality.
The fixed point says there is a self-consistent profile under the assumptions. It does not say the profile is efficient, unique, or easy to find.

title: Backward Induction As Solving The Future First

sections.heading: Start From The Last Real Choice
sections.body: Backward induction is the habit of walking to the end of a game tree before judging the beginning. If a later player will eventually choose between accepting and rejecting an offer, start there. Ask what that player will want at that later point. Then carry that answer one step earlier. The early player should not plan around a later threat or promise unless that later action will still make sense when the time comes.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Time changes strategy because words said early can become empty later. A person may threaten to punish, refuse, walk away, or fight, but the model has to ask whether the person will actually want to do that after the earlier choices have already happened. Backward induction exists to remove plans that depend on later actions no one would carry out. It replaces announced resolve with a step-by-step check of later incentives.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to take the first statement in a sequential game at face value. In everyday life, people often make threats that sound strong because they are spoken early. In the model, early speech does not settle credibility. A later decision maker will face a new choice with the past already fixed. Backward induction asks what that person wants then, not what sounded useful before.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Bargaining
sections.body: Backward induction matters in negotiations, entry deterrence, litigation, war threats, hiring processes, and product launches. Any time a choice today is meant to shape a later response, the later response needs its own incentive check. The same idea appears in computer science when an algorithm solves a finite decision tree from the leaves back to the root. It appears in law and policy when a rule must predict how people will respond after enforcement becomes costly.

applications.body: A lawsuit threat affects settlement only if trial would still be worth pursuing later. The later cost of carrying out the threat shapes the earlier bargain.
Finite decision trees can be solved from the end back to the start. The method is the same plain idea: later values guide earlier choices.

title: Infinite Repetition As The Future Pushing Back

sections.heading: Start From A Relationship That Continues
sections.body: An infinitely repeated game is not about literal immortality. It is about a relationship with no known final round inside the model. A firm expects to meet its rival again. A worker expects future reviews. A neighbor expects tomorrow to arrive after today. Because the relationship continues, today's gain from cheating may come with tomorrow's loss from punishment, distrust, or refusal to cooperate.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: One-shot reasoning can make cooperation look impossible because each person sees a short-term temptation. Repetition changes the calculation. If the future is valuable enough and actions are observed well enough, a player may give up a tempting gain today to protect future payoffs. The concept exists because many social and market settings are not one-time encounters. The same people, firms, or institutions keep meeting, and memory can discipline behavior.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to say repeated play automatically creates cooperation. It does not. The future must matter, the bad action must be noticed, and the punishment must be credible. If players are impatient, if monitoring is noisy, or if punishment hurts the punisher too much, cooperation can break. The repeated-game lesson is not optimism. It is a careful comparison between today's temptation and tomorrow's cost.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Firms
sections.body: The idea matters in workplace trust, online reputation, community rules, supply chains, diplomacy, and climate agreements. It explains how present behavior can be shaped by expected future treatment. In biology, repeated interaction can help explain stable cooperation among organisms under the right conditions. In distributed systems, repeated contact and reputation can discourage harmful behavior when no single central enforcer controls every action.

applications.body: A seller may avoid a short-term scam because bad ratings harm future sales. The future is part of the present payoff calculation, and that only works when buyers can observe enough history to punish bad behavior.

Countries may cooperate when future trade, sanctions, monitoring, and reputation make cheating costly enough. The hard part is making those future responses believable, visible, and worth carrying out after the cheating has already happened.

title: Bayesian Games As Strategy With Hidden Facts

sections.heading: Start From Not Knowing Who You Face
sections.body: A Bayesian game begins when a player must choose without knowing some fact that matters. A bidder may not know other bidders' values. A firm may not know a rival's cost. A negotiator may not know whether the other side is patient or desperate. The model calls these hidden facts types. A type is not a personality label. It is the private information that changes payoffs, choices, or beliefs.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Complete-information games pretend that everyone knows the relevant payoff facts. Many important settings do not look like that. If hidden information changes what a player wants, the strategy must say what each possible type would do. Other players then choose using beliefs about which type they may be facing. Bayesian games exist because uncertainty about people is not a footnote; it changes the action that is best.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to average people together too quickly. If half the sellers have high quality and half have low quality, the buyer does not face one average seller in a simple way. The buyer faces uncertainty, and the seller's action may itself give information. A Bayesian model keeps the hidden states separate long enough to ask how each type acts and how others reason from those possible actions.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Auctions
sections.body: Bayesian games matter in insurance, hiring, medical testing, cybersecurity, diplomacy, and any setting where one side knows something the other side must infer. They also matter for topology-based existence work because beliefs and type-contingent strategies enlarge the space in which fixed-point reasoning may be applied. The math can prove a self-consistent plan exists only after the model has clearly named the hidden facts and the belief structure. If those hidden facts are chosen carelessly, the proof may be clean while the lesson is pointed at the wrong uncertainty.

applications.body: An employer does not observe worker fit directly. Schooling, references, interviews, and trial tasks become actions interpreted through beliefs about hidden ability.
A defender may not know the attacker's type, patience, or target. Defensive choices depend on beliefs about hidden motives and costs.

title: Auctions As Rules For Turning Private Values Into Bids

sections.heading: Start From A Simple Sale With Hidden Values
sections.body: An auction is a rule for deciding who gets an object and what they pay when bidders know their own values better than the seller does. The everyday picture is familiar: people want the same item, but each person has a different willingness to pay. The auction rule turns those private values into public bids. The important point is that a bid is not the same thing as a value. It is an action shaped by the payment rule and by competition.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: If a seller knew everyone's value, selling would be easier. With private values, the rule must draw information out through incentives. In a first-price auction, a high bid raises the chance of winning but also raises the price paid if the bidder wins. In a second-price auction, the payment rule changes that tradeoff. Auction theory exists because allocation, payment, belief, and strategic shading have to be studied together.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to think the highest-value bidder simply says the true value in every auction. That can be wrong. A bidder asks what bid gives the best expected surplus, not what bid sounds honest. Different rules change that calculation. Truthful bidding may be a result under special rules, not a natural default. The course makes the rule visible so the reader can see why bidding changes when payment changes.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Selling Objects
sections.body: Auctions matter anywhere a scarce thing must be assigned under private information: spectrum licenses, online ads, school seats, organ exchange priorities, electricity markets, procurement contracts, and platform rankings. The larger lesson is that rules create behavior. A designer who changes the payment rule, reserve price, ranking formula, or information shown to bidders may change both revenue and who receives the object.

applications.body: Governments use bidding rules to buy work from firms with private costs. The rule affects both the winning firm and how much cost information the bids reveal.
Ad slots and rankings are sold through repeated auctions. The design must account for clicks, quality, private value, and strategic bid shading.

title: Signaling As Making Hidden Information Hard To Fake

sections.heading: Start From A Receiver Who Cannot See The Type
sections.body: Signaling starts with a simple problem: one side knows something and the other side cannot see it directly. A worker may know ability, a seller may know quality, and a firm may know whether it is strong or weak. The receiver observes an action, certificate, price, promise, or other sign. The question is not whether the sign looks impressive. The question is whether different hidden types have different incentives to send it.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Information does not move by magic. If a low-quality seller can cheaply copy the high-quality seller's sign, the sign may not separate anyone. Signaling exists because the model must ask whether imitation is profitable. A separating signal works only when each type prefers the action assigned to that type. A pooling signal leaves types together, so the receiver cannot learn much from the observed action.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to treat a signal as proof. A degree, warranty, public promise, expensive building, or high price may mean something, but only after the incentive check. Who would want to send this sign? Who would find it too costly or not worth copying? If the model skips those questions, it can mistake decoration for information. The receiver learns from incentives, not from the sign's appearance alone.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Education
sections.body: Signaling matters in labor markets, product quality, finance, politics, biology, and online identity. It explains why costly actions can carry information and why cheap labels often fail. In biology, displays can signal fitness when weak types cannot easily fake them. In digital systems, verification badges, deposits, history, or costly commitments can help separate reliable participants from unreliable ones, but only when copying remains unattractive.

applications.body: A long warranty can signal confidence only if low-quality sellers expect it to be too costly. The warranty works through incentives, not words.
Badges, deposits, and verified histories can signal reliability when fake accounts cannot cheaply copy the same pattern, or when copying it would remove the gain from pretending online.

sections.heading: Start From A Fact Everyone May Need To Act On
sections.body: Common knowledge is about public assurance, not just information. A fact can be true, and each person can know it, but that may still be too weak for coordination. Each person may wonder whether others know it, whether others know that others know it, and whether everyone is reasoning from the same starting point. Common knowledge is the strong shared state where this ladder keeps going.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Coordination often requires more than private awareness. If a public rule change is announced to everyone at once, people can act knowing that others heard it too. If the same rule is sent privately to each person, the factual content may be identical, but the strategic effect can differ. Common knowledge exists because strategic action can depend on what people believe about other people's beliefs, not only on the first fact.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to say everyone knows and stop there. Everyone knowing can mean each person separately received the fact. It does not always mean each person knows that the others received it, or that this is itself known, and so on. The higher levels sound abstract, but they answer a practical question: can people safely coordinate because they know the fact is shared?

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Classroom Puzzles
sections.body: Common knowledge matters in financial markets, legal announcements, software protocol changes, traffic conventions, political protests, and team work. Public announcements can move behavior because they change the shared reasoning environment. In topology and fixed-point models, common knowledge can affect which game is being solved: the set of strategies, beliefs, and feasible coordination patterns may change when information is public rather than private. The fact itself is only one part of the object; the public status of the fact can change the strategic space.

applications.body: A protocol update works only when participants can treat the rule and its adoption as shared. Private notice may leave coordination risk.
Public news can move prices not only because traders learn the fact, but because they know other traders learned it too.

title: Utility As A Number That Carries A Ranking

sections.heading: Start From Ranking Before Measuring
sections.body: Utility is easy to misunderstand because it uses numbers. The first idea is not that happiness has been measured like weight or height. The first idea is simpler: if a person ranks one outcome above another, the model can sometimes use numbers to carry that ranking. Higher utility means the model treats the outcome as better for that person inside the problem being studied. The number is a tool for comparison, not a claim that the person's inner life has been fully measured.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Game theory needs payoffs because strategic reasoning compares actions. A firm asks whether one price gives more profit than another. A bidder asks whether winning at a price is better than losing. A negotiator asks whether waiting is better than accepting. Utility gives the model a compact way to make those comparisons. Without it, later tools like best response and equilibrium would have nothing to maximize, and the model would only have loose words like wants or likes.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to treat utility as literal pleasure points. In this course, utility is usually a representation of ranked outcomes or payoffs. That difference matters. If the same ranking can be represented by many different number scales, the reader should not over-read the units. The important question is whether the numbers preserve the comparisons the model needs. A utility number is useful when it makes choices checkable without pretending to describe the whole person.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond The First Model
sections.body: Utility matters in economics, political science, law, computer science, public health, and design because models often need to compare tradeoffs. It also matters in topology and fixed-point existence proofs. A best-response map usually comes from players maximizing payoff over a choice set. If the utility function is continuous and the choice set has the right shape, the mathematics may prove a stable point exists. But the meaning of that point still depends on whether utility captured the right tradeoff.

applications.body: A design model must say what users are trading off, such as speed, privacy, cost, or ease. Utility records the tradeoff so choices can be compared.
Existence results often need a well-behaved payoff function. The proof may be formal, but the payoff meaning comes from the modeled ranking.

title: Expected Utility As Choosing Under Risk

sections.heading: Start From Not Knowing Which Outcome Will Happen
sections.body: Expected utility begins when a choice leads to several possible outcomes. A person may buy insurance, enter an auction, invest in a project, or choose a route before knowing the weather. The model cannot pretend the uncertainty is gone. It lists the possible outcomes, assigns probabilities, and averages the utility of those outcomes using those probabilities. The point is not to predict the exact outcome. The point is to compare choices before the uncertainty is resolved.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Many game-theory choices are made before a player knows what kind of opponent, value, cost, or state of the world they face. Expected utility gives the player a way to choose anyway. A bidder compares the chance of winning and the payoff if they win. A firm compares possible demand states. A player in a Bayesian game compares payoffs across possible types. Without expected utility, the course could not connect beliefs to action in a disciplined way.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to average money or outcomes directly without asking what the person values. If a person dislikes risk, a fifty-fifty chance of gaining or losing the same amount may not feel neutral in the model. Expected utility averages utility, not just dollars. Another mistake is to treat the expected value as the thing that will happen. It is a comparison device before the outcome is known, not a promise that the average result will appear.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Lotteries
sections.body: Expected utility matters in insurance, medicine, finance, safety engineering, artificial intelligence, and public decisions under risk. It is also part of the bridge to topology-based equilibrium proofs in games with uncertainty. A player's best response can depend on an expected payoff over unknown states. If those expected payoff functions are well behaved, fixed-point methods can sometimes prove a self-consistent profile exists. The proof rests on the ordinary idea that uncertain outcomes still need a choice rule.

applications.body: A treatment choice may compare possible benefits and harms before anyone knows which patient outcome will occur. Expected utility makes that uncertainty explicit.
An agent choosing under uncertainty needs a rule for trading off possible future states. Expected utility is one plain way to build that rule.

title: Strategic Form Games As A Clean Table Of Mutual Dependence

sections.heading: Start From Choices Made Without Seeing Each Other
sections.body: A strategic form game is the course's compact table for situations where each player's payoff depends on the combination of everyone's choices. The everyday picture is two firms setting prices, two students choosing whether to contribute to a project, or two countries choosing policies without first seeing the other's exact move. The table is not decoration. It is the model's claim about who the players are, what choices they have, and what each outcome gives them.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Game theory needs a way to hold the whole strategic situation in one place. If my payoff depends only on my action, ordinary individual choice may be enough. If my payoff also depends on your action, the model needs a table or function that records the joint effect. Strategic form exists because dependence must be made visible before concepts like dominance, best response, and Nash equilibrium can be applied. The table turns a story into something that can be checked.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to fill in a payoff matrix as if it were obvious. The hardest part is often deciding what belongs in the table. Are players choosing prices, quantities, entry, effort, votes, or messages? Are payoffs money, utility, market share, reputation, or some mix? A strategic form game is only as good as those choices. A neat table can still be wrong if it hides timing, information, or a missing option.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Simple Matrices
sections.body: Strategic form matters in economics, security, traffic routing, platform design, voting, and biology because it provides the first clean picture of mutual dependence. It also matters for topology because many equilibrium existence proofs start with a strategy space and payoff functions defined over action profiles. The fixed point is meaningful only after the strategic form has named the space and payoffs. A poor representation gives a poor map, even if the theorem is correct.

applications.body: A defender's best plan depends on the attacker's plan, and the attacker's payoff depends on the defense. A table makes that dependence inspectable.
Competing traits can be modeled by payoffs that depend on the traits around them. The table records fitness consequences from combinations, not isolated actions.

title: Dominance As Removing A Move With No Good Defense

sections.heading: Start From Comparing Two Choices
sections.body: Dominance starts with a direct comparison. Take one player and compare two possible actions while holding fixed each possible thing the others might do. If one action is never worse and sometimes better, the worse action has no good defense in the model. The player should not need a detailed prediction about others to reject it. The dominated move is bad across the relevant cases.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Before solving a whole game, the course often asks whether some choices can be ruled out immediately. Dominance gives a first cleanup tool. It does not require a full equilibrium story. It only asks whether one action loses to another action across the board. This matters because large games can contain options that distract the reader. Removing a dominated action can reveal the real strategic pressure that remains.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to say an action is dominated because it looks unattractive in one likely case. That is not enough. Dominance is a strong claim about all relevant opponent actions. Another mistake is to treat weak and strict dominance as the same. Weak comparisons can be delicate because deleting a weakly dominated action may change what remains in ways that depend on the order of deletion or on fine details of belief.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Classroom Tables
sections.body: Dominance matters in contract choices, bidding, product strategy, voting rules, and policy design because it identifies options that no reasonable model participant should need. In computer science and operations work, similar pruning ideas remove impossible or inferior branches before a search continues. In topology-heavy equilibrium work, dominance does not replace fixed-point reasoning, but it can simplify the strategy space before asking whether a stable point exists.

applications.body: A planner can discard choices that are never better than another available choice. That reduces clutter before deeper reasoning begins, while still forcing the planner to prove the comparison across all relevant cases.

A voting rule can create dominated voting actions. Finding them shows where the rule asks people to act strategically against their sincere ranking, and where a simpler rule might remove needless manipulation.

title: Rationalizability As Asking What Belief Could Make This Sensible

sections.heading: Start From A Move That Looks Odd
sections.body: Rationalizability begins with a generous everyday question about people choosing under uncertainty. Suppose a player chooses an action that is not immediately ruled out. Could that action be the best response to some reasonable belief about what others will do? If yes, the action has a possible strategic explanation. It may not be the final prediction, and it may not be part of a Nash equilibrium, but it is not foolish inside every possible belief story.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Dominance removes actions that have no defense. Rationalizability studies the actions that survive a belief-based defense. The concept exists because a player's choice can only be judged after saying what they think others might do. A move that looks strange against one opponent action may be sensible against another expected action. Rationalizability keeps belief inside the analysis instead of pretending the analyst already knows the correct forecast.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to treat rationalizable as meaning likely, correct, or socially good. It means the action can be made optimal under some allowable belief. That is a weaker and broader idea than equilibrium. Another mistake is to let any wild belief justify anything. The course still disciplines beliefs through the deletion process and through the assumption that other players are also reasoning about best responses.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Early Solution Concepts
sections.body: Rationalizability matters in legal reasoning, market interpretation, political analysis, and machine learning because observed behavior often has to be interpreted before the analyst knows the actor's beliefs. It also matters near topology because equilibrium can be seen as a stricter self-consistency point, while rationalizability marks a larger set of choices that survive belief-based reasoning. The distinction helps readers understand why fixed-point equilibrium is not the only way to talk about strategic plausibility.

applications.body: An action that seems unreasonable may make sense under one party's belief about the other party. The belief story must still be disciplined.
When agents learn from each other, a move may be sensible under a mistaken but plausible belief. Rationalizability separates that from pure error.

title: Best Response As The Move That Fits A Belief

sections.heading: Start From Freezing The Other Side
sections.body: A best response is the choice that gives a player the highest payoff after the player fixes a belief about what others will do. The idea is ordinary. If a rival sets a high price, one action may be best. If the rival sets a low price, another action may be best. A move is not best in the air. It is best against some expectation, opponent action, or probability story.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Best response is the hinge between individual choice and strategic prediction. Each player is still choosing for themselves, but the choice depends on others. Nash equilibrium is built by putting best responses together. Bayesian Nash uses best responses by type. Repeated games ask whether a continuation plan remains a best response after histories. The concept exists because strategic reasoning needs a local test before it can build a whole-system stability claim.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to call an action best without saying best against what. A price, bid, route, message, or threat can be good under one belief and poor under another. Another mistake is to think a best response must be unique. Sometimes several actions tie. That tie can be important, especially when mixed strategies or equilibrium selection enter. The best-response question is precise because it names the comparison being made.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Game Tables
sections.body: Best responses matter in traffic systems, platform design, pricing, negotiation, cybersecurity, and political campaigns. They are also central to fixed-point reasoning in topology. A best-response correspondence maps what others do into the set of actions a player is willing to choose. An equilibrium is a place where all those response maps fit together. The mathematical theorem may sound abstract, but it is built from the everyday act of asking what choice fits a belief.

applications.body: A driver's best route depends on where other drivers are expected to go. A route can be best at one traffic level and poor at another.
A defender's best response depends on the expected attack path. Changing beliefs about the attacker can change the defense.

title: Mixed Strategies As Randomness With A Strategic Job

sections.heading: Start From Being Too Predictable
sections.body: A mixed strategy means choosing randomly according to a planned probability. The everyday reason is not confusion. It is that predictability can be exploited. A tennis player who always serves left lets the returner prepare. A security team that always patrols the same route invites avoidance. Randomness can be useful when the other side benefits from knowing exactly what you will do.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Some games have no stable prediction in pure actions. If one player picks rock, the other wants paper; if paper, then scissors; if scissors, then rock. The cycle means no fixed pure move survives. Mixed strategies let the model search for stability in probabilities instead. A player may randomize so that the opponent is kept indifferent among certain actions, removing the profitable predictable response.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to treat mixing as a player being careless or unable to decide. In the model, mixing can be deliberate. Another mistake is to think any random probabilities work. Equilibrium mixing has a reason: the probabilities must make opponents willing to play the actions they are supposed to use. The exact numbers carry incentive work. They are not decorative uncertainty pasted onto a deterministic story.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Games Of Chance
sections.body: Mixed strategies matter in sports, inspections, cybersecurity, military planning, pricing, and platform moderation. They also matter for topology because probability mixtures can make strategy sets convex, which is one reason fixed-point existence theorems can apply. The mathematical convenience has a plain meaning: the player is allowed to choose a probability plan rather than only a single action. That expanded space can create a stable point where no pure action profile could.

applications.body: A regulator may randomize inspection times so firms cannot safely hide violations around a known schedule. The randomness creates discipline because the firm cannot make one clean plan around a predictable visit.

Rotating defenses can prevent attackers from exploiting a fixed pattern. The mix must still fit the cost and protection tradeoff, because random movement without purpose can waste effort and leave weak spots exposed.

title: Subgame Perfection As Credibility At Every Later Point

sections.heading: Start From A Plan That Reaches The Future
sections.body: Subgame perfection asks whether an equilibrium plan remains sensible after every later point that could be reached. A plan can be a Nash equilibrium because nobody wants to change at the very start, yet it may rely on a threat that would be foolish later. Subgame perfection tightens the test. It says the strategy must pass the no-deviation logic not only from the beginning, but also inside each proper continuation of the game.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Sequential games need a stronger credibility check than one-shot strategic-form games. A firm may threaten a price war after entry. A negotiator may threaten to reject a future offer. A parent, manager, or government may announce a punishment. The model has to ask whether that future action will be worthwhile once the later moment arrives. Subgame perfection exists because early incentives and later incentives can differ.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to accept any Nash equilibrium in a game tree as a serious prediction. Some Nash equilibria survive only because they contain off-path threats that no one would actually carry out. Subgame perfection rejects those empty threats when the relevant subgame can be evaluated. It does not solve every dynamic information problem, but it teaches the reader to inspect credibility after histories, not just at the root.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Entry Games
sections.body: Subgame perfection matters in bargaining, regulation, litigation, industrial organization, diplomacy, and organizational discipline. It also links to topology and fixed-point thinking through the larger family of equilibrium refinements. Existence of a stable point is not enough when the point is supported by unbelievable future behavior. The refinement asks whether the fixed point has the right internal structure along the time path.

applications.body: A regulator's announced punishment shapes behavior only if the regulator will still want to impose it later. Credibility changes compliance because firms reason about the later enforcement choice, not only the written rule.
A threat can deter action only when carrying it out later is believable. Subgame perfection makes that future check explicit and separates real deterrence from language that sounds strong early.
